**The Weight of the Unseen**

The first time I noticed the silence, I was twenty-three, standing in a subway station at 2:17 AM. The last train had long since departed, and the fluorescent lights buzzed like a swarm of invisible bees. There was no one else there—no straggling commuters, no drunk college students, no homeless man curled against the bench. Just me, the flickering ads for dental floss and life insurance, and the oppressive weight of the air.

It wasn’t the absence of sound that struck me. Cities are never truly silent; there’s always the hum of electricity, the distant wail of a siren, the creak of metal expanding and contracting. No, it was the absence of *expectation*. For the first time in my life, there was no one watching. No one waiting. No one who would care if I sat down on the cold tile, or screamed, or simply disappeared into the tunnels.

I didn’t do any of those things. I just stood there, feeling the strange lightness of being unseen. It was terrifying. It was freeing.

---

We spend our lives performing. From the moment we learn to smile for a parent’s camera, we are actors in a play with no script, improvising our way through scenes we didn’t audit for. *How are you?* Fine. *What do you do?* Something socially acceptable. *Do you like it?* Of course. The answers are pre-approved, the emotions pre-packaged. We learn early that the truth is a luxury, and authenticity is a risk.

But who are we when no one is watching?

That question has haunted me for years. It’s why I took to writing in the first place—not because I had stories to tell, but because I needed to hear my own voice without the distortion of other people’s expectations. On paper, I could be honest. On paper, I could be ugly, petty, cruel, or absurd, and no one would flinch. The page doesn’t judge. The page doesn’t love you either, but at least it doesn’t lie.

---

There’s a myth that solitude is for the lonely, that those who seek it out are running from something. But solitude isn’t the absence of people; it’s the absence of *noise*. And noise isn’t just sound. It’s the chatter of social media, the pressure to have an opinion on everything, the exhausting performance of being *on* all the time. We drown out the quiet because we’re afraid of what we’ll hear in it.

I once spent a week in a cabin in the woods with no phone, no internet, and no clock. The first two days were agony. I paced. I talked to myself. I considered walking to the nearest town just to hear another human voice. But by the third day, something shifted. The silence stopped feeling like a void and started feeling like a space. My thoughts, usually so cluttered, began to unspool like yarn. I remembered dreams I’d forgotten. I cried for no reason. I laughed at nothing. And then, on the fifth day, I wrote a story that felt like it came from somewhere deeper than me.

It wasn’t a good story. But it was *true*.

---

Truth is overrated, though. Or at least, that’s what we tell ourselves when the alternative is uncomfortable. We prefer our illusions. The illusion that we are in control. The illusion that we are good. The illusion that we are special. The internet has turned us all into narcissists and critics at once—we demand to be seen, but we tear apart those who are.

I once posted a piece of writing online that was raw, unfiltered, and deeply personal. It was about grief, about the way loss doesn’t hit you like a wave but like a slow, suffocating tide. I hesitated before hitting *publish*, but I told myself that honesty was brave. The responses were… mixed. Some people called it beautiful. Others said it was self-indulgent. One person commented, *This is why no one reads your stuff.*

I deleted it within an hour.

The thing about vulnerability is that it’s only celebrated when it’s performed *correctly*. We love a good tragic backstory, as long as it’s packaged neatly and tied with a bow of redemption. But real grief? Real mess? That’s not content. That’s just… sad.

---

And yet, we crave the mess. We crave the real. That’s why we’re drawn to art that makes us feel something, even if that something is discomfort. That’s why we fall in love with people who don’t play by the rules. That’s why, when we’re alone in our cars, we sing at the top of our lungs, or cry, or scream, or do nothing at all.

There’s a freedom in being unseen. But there’s also a terror. Because if no one is watching, then your choices don’t matter. And if your choices don’t matter, then what’s the point of anything?

I think this is why some people fill their lives with noise—to avoid the existential dread of irrelevance. If you’re always busy, always needed, always *doing*, then you don’t have to ask yourself why you’re doing it. But the quiet doesn’t go away. It waits. And eventually, it finds you.

---

It found me again last winter, during a snowstorm. The power went out, and for the first time in years, the world went dark. No screens, no notifications, no hum of the refrigerator. Just the sound of wind shaking the windows and the faint, rhythmic *drip… drip… drip* of melting snow.

I sat by the fireplace (yes, I’m lucky enough to have one) and stared into the flames. I didn’t read. I didn’t think. I just… existed. And for the first time in a long time, I didn’t feel like I was performing. I wasn’t a writer. I wasn’t a daughter. I wasn’t a friend. I was just a person, in a room, in the dark.

It was the most peaceful I’d felt in years.

---

But peace isn’t the same as happiness. Peace doesn’t solve anything. It just gives you the clarity to see the problems you’ve been too distracted to notice.

For me, that clarity came with a cost. I realized I’d spent years chasing validation—from editors, from readers, from friends, from strangers on the internet. I’d tied my self-worth to external approval, and no matter how much I got, it was never enough. Because the truth is, you can’t fill a hole with other people’s opinions. It’s like trying to quench thirst with saltwater.

So I stopped posting as much. I stopped seeking out reviews. I stopped measuring my life in likes and shares. And at first, it felt like I was disappearing. But then, slowly, I started to reappear—to myself.

---

This isn’t a manifesto. I’m not advocating for a life of isolation or rejection of the modern world. I still check my phone too often. I still care what people think. I still perform. But now, I’m trying to carve out more moments of quiet. Moments where I’m not *producing* or *consuming* or *optimizing*—just *being*.

It’s not easy. The world doesn’t reward stillness. Capitalism thrives on our restlessness. Social media thrives on our outrage. Even our hobbies have become side hustles. We’re not allowed to do things just because they bring us joy. Everything has to *mean* something.

But what if the meaning is just… the doing?

What if the point of writing isn’t to be read, but to write? What if the point of painting isn’t to be seen, but to paint? What if the point of living isn’t to be remembered, but to live?

---

I had a teacher in college who once said, *The problem with modern life is that we’ve confused motion with progress.* We think that if we’re not moving, we’re failing. But sometimes, the most radical act is to stand still.

I think about that subway station sometimes—the one where I first noticed the silence. I was twenty-three then. I’m older now. I’ve lived more. I’ve lost more. I’ve loved more. And I’ve learned that the scariest and most beautiful thing about life is that no one is the protagonist. We’re all just extras in each other’s stories.

But here’s the secret: *You’re the protagonist of your own.*

Even when no one is watching.

Even when no one cares.

You still get to decide what kind of story you’re in.

---

And maybe that’s the point. Maybe the weight of the unseen isn’t a burden, but a gift. Maybe the silence isn’t empty. Maybe it’s full of all the things we’ve been too loud to hear.

Maybe we’re not supposed to fill it.

Maybe we’re supposed to listen.
